records.title: Mercy Introduces the Quranic Description of God

fields.label: Discovery statement
fields.value: The Quran opens by repeatedly describing God with al-Rahman/al-Rahim, placing mercy/compassion at the front of its theological presentation.

fields.label: Original-language evidence
fields.value: Arabic: al-Rahman (الرحمن), al-Rahim (الرحيم), both from R-H-M semantic family.

fields.label: Supporting evidence
fields.value: Direct evidence: 1:1 and 1:3 repeat the paired descriptors.

fields.label: Explanation / carry-forward
fields.value: Mercy must be studied alongside later judgment language; no claim yet that mercy overrides justice.

records.title: God Is Lord of All Worlds and Master of Judgment

fields.label: Discovery statement
fields.value: God is identified as Lord of the worlds and Master/Owner of the Day of Judgment, joining universal sovereignty, mercy, and judgment.

fields.label: Explanation / carry-forward
fields.value: Creates the early Mercy ↔ Judgment theological relationship.

records.title: Worship and Ultimate Dependence Are Directed to God

fields.label: Discovery statement
fields.value: The prayer directs worship and appeal for help to God with emphatic object-fronting.

fields.label: Original-language evidence
fields.value: iyyaka na'budu; wa-iyyaka nasta'in. Iyyaka is fronted for emphasis/exclusivity.

fields.label: Explanation / carry-forward
fields.value: Later passages on intercession, prophets, Jesus, angels, and shirk must be tested against this baseline.

records.title: Correct Guidance Must Come From God

fields.label: Discovery statement
fields.value: The worshiper petitions God for guidance to al-sirat al-mustaqim, establishing divine guidance as necessary.

fields.label: Explanation / carry-forward
fields.value: Open question: what exactly constitutes the straight path?

records.title: Three Path/Destination Categories Open the Quran

fields.label: Discovery statement
fields.value: The straight path is associated with those favored by God and contrasted with those under displeasure and those astray.

fields.label: Evidence classification
fields.value: 🟢 Direct Textual Statement / 🔵 Strong Textual Pattern

fields.label: Explanation / carry-forward
fields.value: Surah 1 itself does not identify the latter groups as Jews or Christians; later commentary must not be retrojected into the verse.

fields.label: Discovery statement
fields.value: Surah 1 asks for guidance and contrasts paths; Surah 2 immediately identifies the Book as guidance and contrasts believing, rejecting, and hypocritical responses.

fields.label: Explanation / carry-forward
fields.value: Structural relationship, not a claim of later editorial intent beyond textual sequence.

records.title: Al-Baqarah Is Structured Around Human Response to Divine Guidance

fields.label: Discovery statement
fields.value: The surah begins by identifying the Book as guidance after Al-Fatihah’s request, repeatedly tests responses to revelation, and closes with “we hear and obey.”

fields.label: Original-language evidence
fields.value: hudan; samiʿnā wa-aṭaʿnā; recurring qalb/īmān/kufr/taqwā vocabulary.

fields.label: Supporting evidence
fields.value: The guidance-response pattern spans the whole surah across theology, narrative, ritual, ethics, family law, warfare, commerce, and prayer.

fields.label: Explanation / carry-forward
fields.value: Primary structural synthesis for completed Surah 2.

records.title: Prayer for Divine Guidance Onto God's Path

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: Both ask God to teach/guide onto the right path. Leave open for later definition of 'straight path'.

fields.label: Status rule
fields.value: preliminary classifications remain revisable only by later evidence under the existing record; IDs remain permanent.

packets.title: S001 Al-Fatihah
paragraphs: Verses in standard Kufan count: 7 (basmala counted as v.1)
Traditional chronology: Meccan — commonly listed among the earliest; exact serial number in revelation lists varies (often ~5th). Certainty: traditional, not internally dated by the surah.
Checkpoint: Complete short-surah packet (CUM-00 system test)

Al-Fatihah is a short liturgical unit of praise and petition. It names God, ascribes praise and mercy and eschatological authority to God, then switches from third-person description to second-person address: exclusive worship and help-seeking, then a request for guidance on a path defined by favor and by two rejected alternatives (those subjected to anger; those who go astray).

The surah does not narrate an event, name Muhammad, name Jesus, name earlier books, or issue a legal ruling. Later Islamic practice treats it as the required opening of ritual prayer. That liturgical use is Level 3–4 (early/classical tradition), not a Level 1 statement inside these seven verses.
Two-movement structure is the most economical reading of the Arabic:
A. vv.1–4 — Identification and praise of God (basmala + hamd + mercy + eschatological sovereignty).
B. vv.5–7 — Address to God: exclusive worship and aid; petition for guidance; triple path-classification (favored / angered-upon / astray).

v.5 is the hinge: iyyaka (“You [alone]”) fronted twice. Classical tafsir often splits the surah as “half for God, half for the servant.” That split is a later pedagogical frame (Level 4) that maps reasonably onto the grammar but is not stated by the text.

Verse-count dispute: most printed muṣḥafs following the Kufan tradition count the basmala as 1:1 and close at seven verses. Some other counting traditions treat the basmala as a header and split v.7, still totaling seven. This is a recitation/codex convention issue, not a different wording of the prayer body. Classification: OPEN on which count is “original”; DIRECT that the wording block is stable.

“In the name of Allah, the Raḥmān, the Raḥīm.” Formula of invocation. Allah is the proper name used throughout the Quran for God. Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm share root r-ḥ-m (mercy; also raḥim, womb). Traditional distinction: Raḥmān as expansive/universal mercy, Raḥīm as enduring or particular mercy. That distinction is classical exegesis (Level 4), widely repeated, not parsed by 1:1 itself. DIRECT: God is named and two mercy epithets are applied.

“The praise is for Allah, rabb of the ʿālamīn.” Al-ḥamd is praise/commendation with the definite article (the praise, not merely a praise). Rabb covers lord, owner, fosterer, master — not only “deity.” ʿĀlamīn is plural of ʿālam (world/realm/class of beings). English “worlds / universe / all beings” all sit inside the semantic range. DIRECT: praise is ascribed to Allah as rabb of the ʿālamīn.
Repeats the two mercy names without Allah. Reinforces mercy after lordship. DIRECT repetition. SYNTHESIS: mercy is not a minor attribute in this opening unit.

Two canonical readings of the first word exist: mālik (owner/possessor) and malik (king). Both are among the accepted qirāʾāt. Yawm al-dīn: dīn here is widely read as requital/judgment rather than “religion” in the modern institutional sense, though dīn’s Quranic range includes religion, debt, custom, and requital. Immediate phrase is eschatological. DIRECT: God is mālik or malik of the Day of dīn. OPEN: whether the authorial/performative intention was one reading only.

Object fronted twice with iyyāka (“You”). Naʿbudu from ʿ-b-d (serve/worship/enslave oneself to). Nastaʿīn from ʿ-w-n (seek help). First-person plural. The grammar strongly marks exclusivity of the object; English “alone” is an interpretive tightening that most translators add because of the fronting. DIRECT: the speakers worship and seek help from the addressee. STRONG PATTERN (grammar): exclusivity of that object. The speakers are not identified by name.

“Guide us (to/on) the straight path.” Ihdinā is a request for hidāyah (guidance). Ṣirāṭ is a path/road (loanword likely from Latin via Greek/Aramaic strata of late antique Near East — linguistic history, not a Level 1 theological claim). Mustaqīm: straight, upright, correct. DIRECT: the speakers ask God to guide them on a straight path.
1:7  ṣirāṭa lladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim ghayri l-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-lā l-ḍāllīn

The path is defined by three groups: (1) those You have favored; (2) not those angered-upon; (3) nor those who go astray. Anʿamta is second-person: God is the subject of favor. Al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim is a passive participle plus preposition: “those upon whom anger has fallen.” The text does not name the agent of anger in this clause, though the surah’s addressee is God. Al-ḍāllīn: those who stray/err. DIRECT: three-way classification of paths/people. The Quran in this surah does not name Jews, Christians, or any ethnicity. Identification of group (2) with Jews and group (3) with Christians is a widespread traditional tafsir claim (Level 3–4) and is audited as QCA-0002.
Marks the object as exclusive focus; strongest grammatical basis for “You alone.”
vv.1–4 describe God; vv.5–7 address God. Standard hymnic move.
Does not say “those You are angry with” in so many words; agent is implicit.
mālik vs malik — both canonical; sense adjacent (owner vs king) not opposite.
naʿbudu / nastaʿīn / ihdinā — communal or generic “we,” not specified.
Material splits worth recording (not every synonym).
SI, Pickthall keep Allah; Arberry, Haleem often God
Proper name vs generic English theos/god convention. Not a doctrinal split in 1:1–2.
SI: Entirely / Especially Merciful; Haleem: Lord of Mercy / Giver of Mercy; Pickthall: Beneficent / Merciful; YA: Most Gracious / Most Merciful; Arberry: Merciful / Compassionate
All render mercy. The SI/Haleem extra precision is interpretive, not forced by morphology alone.
YA unpacks rabb; others keep Lord.
Plural worlds/beings is safer than a modern “universe” as a single cosmos.
Reflects the qira'ah and the translator’s pick. Record both readings.
Requital sense is strong here; “religion” would under-read yawm.
earn Thine anger / go astray; those who evoke anger
None of the core five insert “Jews” or “Christians” in the translation line.

God is one addressee, merciful, praiseworthy, lord of the worlds, and eschatological judge/owner. Worship and help-seeking are directed to that addressee. Human need for guidance is assumed. Moral/religious space is divided into favored, angered-upon, and astray. Salvation language in the later systematic sense (atonement, justification) is not present. Intercession is not mentioned. Muhammad is not mentioned.

At this stage only forward pointers, not yet investigated in-project: rabb al-ʿālamīn recurs often; al-Raḥmān is a major name (e.g. Surah 55); ṣirāṭ mustaqīm recurs; yawm al-dīn and dīn-as-requital recur; exclusive worship theme will be tested against later legal and polemical passages. No internal tension (QI) is claimed from S001 alone.

Psalmic praise of the LORD as king and refuge (e.g. Psalm 24; 86; 145). Petition “teach me thy way / lead me” (Psalm 25; 27). The Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13 / Luke 11:2–4): address to God, name/hallowing, petition for divine action, moral path. These are structural and thematic analogies. S001 does not cite them. No shared wording that would demonstrate literary dependence has been established here.

AGREEMENT (limited, thematic): a merciful, praiseworthy God; prayer for guidance; coming judgment. PARTIAL AGREEMENT with biblical prayer: communal petition to one God, without the Lord’s Prayer’s “Father” language and without S001’s three-group path formula. OMISSION: no Jesus, no Spirit, no covenant name YHWH, no Israel, no church. DIRECT CONTRADICTION: none declared from S001 alone. See QB-0001.

If the traditional Meccan early dating is accepted, the unit is a short monotheistic prayer in a polytheistic cultic environment. The text itself does not date itself. Pre-Islamic Arabic already used Allah for a high god; the Quranic move is to attach exclusive worship and eschatological ownership to that name. Certainty on extra-textual setting: traditional + historically plausible; not proven by S001 wording.
No narrative in this surah. No finding.
Primary data: names, mercy, lordship, judgment-day sovereignty, exclusive worship/help.
No finding on mechanism. The surah is itself treated by Muslims as revealed speech; that claim is external to these verses.
Guidance requested; favor mentioned; no atonement mechanics.
Astray / angered-upon imply failure; no Adamic fall.
Yawm al-din named; paradise/hell not described.
No explicit claim to confirm or replace earlier books.
S001 is a two-movement praise-and-petition unit directing exclusive worship and help-seeking to Allah
1:4 has two canonical readings, malik and malik, with adjacent not opposite senses
Kufan verse count treats basmala as 1:1; other counts exist; wording of the prayer body is the same
1:7 names no ethnicity or religion; “Jews / Christians” reading is later tafsir
Fatiha and biblical prayer (Psalms / Lord’s Prayer): shared petition-to-one-God genre without demonstrated dependence or contradiction
No finding in this unit. No QI issued.
“Islam and Christianity worship exactly the same conception of God.”
OPEN. S001 describes a single merciful eschatological Lord. That is compatible with overlap and insufficient to prove identity of conception. Later Christology/tawhid passages required.
“Quran 1:7 refers to Jews as those under anger and Christians as those who go astray.”
Not a Level 1 Quranic statement. Widespread in hadith/tafsir (Level 3–4). Text itself is unnamed groups. Status: claim originates in tradition, not in the wording of 1:7.

First-pass entries logged in Registers_Master.xlsx sheet Dictionary: Allah, Rabb, Rahman, Rahim, Hamd, Alamin, Malik, Malik_king, Yawm, Din, Ibadah, Istiana, Sirat, Mustaqim, Anama, Maghdub, Dallin, Iyyaka.
God/Allah dossier opened with S001 profile. Jesus dossier remains a shell. Muhammad dossier not opened (figure unnamed).
QURAN qira'at + MODERN ACADEMIC / CLASSICAL description of readings
HADITH / FIQH — not used as Level 1

No historically testable event-claim inside S001 (no battle, no place-name, no dated miracle). Liturgical use in the 7th-century community is historically plausible and universally claimed in Islamic sources; not independently documented by a dated non-Muslim source for this specific prayer in the 610s. Classification: plausible but unverified extra-textually.

Al-Fatihah, on its own wording, is a monotheistic praise-petition: Allah is lord of the worlds, merciful, and sovereign of the Day of requital; the speakers worship and seek help from that God alone and ask to be guided on the path of those God has favored, not the path of the angered-upon or the astray. It does not name the Prophet, Jesus, earlier scripture, or any people. Later tradition supplies liturgical function and a common identification of the last two groups; those supplies are recorded, not merged into Level 1.
• Will later surahs name the maghdub and dallin?
• How will rabb, dīn, ṣirāṭ, and raḥmah be specified or restricted?
• Does exclusive istiʿānah survive later passages that speak of seeking means or the Prophet’s role?
• How does yawm al-dīn relate to detailed judgment scenes still ahead?

kjv.text: Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths.
Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day.

bsb.text: Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths.
Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; all day long I wait for You.

kjv.text: Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul.
O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me.
Yea, let none that wait on thee be ashamed: let them be ashamed which transgress without cause.
Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths.
Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day.
Remember, O LORD, thy tender mercies and thy lovingkindnesses; for they have been ever of old.
Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness’ sake, O LORD.
Good and upright is the LORD: therefore will he teach sinners in the way.
The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way.
All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant and his testimonies.
For thy name’s sake, O LORD, pardon mine iniquity; for it is  great.
What man is he that feareth the LORD? him shall he teach in the way that he shall choose.
His soul shall dwell at ease; and his seed shall inherit the earth.
The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant.
Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.
Turn thee unto me, and have mercy upon me; for I am desolate and afflicted.
The troubles of my heart are enlarged: O bring thou me out of my distresses.
Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins.
Consider mine enemies; for they are many; and they hate me with cruel hatred.
O keep my soul, and deliver me: let me not be ashamed; for I put my trust in thee.
Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee.
Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.

bsb.text: To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul;
in You, my God, I trust. Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me.
Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who engage in treachery without cause will be disgraced.
Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths.
Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; all day long I wait for You.
Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age.
Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD.
Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way.
He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way.
All the LORD’s ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.
For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great.
Who is the man who fears the LORD? He will instruct him in the path chosen for him.
His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land.
The LORD confides in those who fear Him, and reveals His covenant to them.
My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh.
Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted.
The troubles of my heart increase; free me from my distress.
Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins.
Consider my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with vicious hatred.
Guard my soul and deliver me; let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in You.
May integrity and uprightness preserve me, because I wait for You.
Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.

kjv.text: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is  in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

bsb.text: So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name.
Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. ’

kjv.text: And he said unto them, When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth.
Give us day by day our daily bread.
And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil.

bsb.text: So Jesus told them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come.
Give us each day our daily bread.
And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation. ’”

kjv.text: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

bsb.text: Then God said, “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness, to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth itself and every creature that crawls upon it.”
So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

kjv.text: And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.
And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.

bsb.text: And by the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on that day He rested from all His work.
Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on that day He rested from all the work of creation that He had accomplished.
